EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. Many locations across the Oklahoma Panhandle observed wind gusts o 60mph or greater. These strong winds brought blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions as well. Several wildfires developed due to the dry grasses, low relative humidity and high wind gusts. One wildfire in Beaver County burned into Kansas and consumed over 200,000 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Ranger Road fire ignited during the morning of February 17th near Highway 64, one mile southeast of Beaver, Oklahoma. This fire burned 283,283 acres across Oklahoma and Kansas. The fire was fueled by dormant, dry grasses and brush, driven by wind gusts of 60-70 mph and extremely low humidity (10-15%). These conditions created a fast fire environment, allowing the blaze to explode in size���growing from ignition to 15,000 acres in one hour to over 145,000 acres in just nine hours. It rapidly crossed the state line into Clark, Comanche, and Meade counties in Kansas. With strong wind gusts, this helped not only to spread the fire but limited aerial firefighting operations and complicated suppression efforts during the first stages of the fire's expansion. The cause is undetermined.  A firefighter was injured from being burned. In addition, a fire truck from Rosston Fire overturned in Beaver County and three fire fighters were injured, including one that suffered from 2nd and 3rd degree burns and broke his leg. There were 926 primary homes, 2 schools, and commercial/government buildings threatened. Evacuations: Mandatory evacuations for about 771 people that may have covered KS as well.  Gate and Knowles had evacuations on Feb 17th, and numerous outbuildings were destroyed in the fire.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Stevens Fire ignited around 11:45 a.m. on February 17, 2026, approximately seven miles northwest of Hooker, Oklahoma, in Texas County. The fire burned 12,894 acres and was caused by human activities. Smoke from this fire reduced visibility along US Highway 54, which resulted in a seven vehicle accident and additional fire start(which became the Side Road Fire). Mandatory evacuations occurred for the town of Tyrone on the 17th and were lifted by the morning of February 21st. US Highway 54 was closed between Tyrone and Hooker due to smoke and fire activity.  Five structures were burned: 4 barns and one house per OEMA. About 263 homes were threatened by this fire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dry weather continued on February 18th and 19th. Winds were gusty but remained below high wind thresholds. Southwesterly sustained winds of 25-35mph occurred with gusts up to 45 or 55mph. However, given the dry fuels and low relative humidity, this allowed for additional wildfires to develop across portions of the Oklahoma Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Morning Fire burned 820 acres.  It started near Highway 83 and County Road 21, about nine miles northwest of Balko. This fire occurred as a result of a car accident that occurred just after 9am on February 19th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dry conditions occurred across the Oklahoma Panhandle to start February. A cold front dropped south through the region on February 10th and brought breezy winds and at least elevated fire weather conditions to the region. This resulted in the development of two wildfires in Beaver County, Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Flat Tire wildfire ignited at approximately 11:35 a.m. on February 10, 2026, in Beaver County, Oklahoma. The fire was located south of the town of Turpin, or 1/4 of a mile east of the intersection NS123 and EW10. It burned in and around the Beaver River bottom area. This fire was human caused. Officials noted that a flat tire had blown off and sparked, which caused the ignition. The fire was fueled by exceptional fuel loading in the county. The fire burned 1,983 acres. No damage to homes or major structures occurred with this fire. However, US Highway 83 was closed on February 10th in Turpin to US Highway 412 due to the fire.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The No Tire wildfire started nearly the same location as the Flat Tire fire occurred.  It started further down the road as the car that ignited the Flat Tire fire continued to travel on the rim with no tire attached, and the rim would go on to set a new separate ignition point than the Flat Tire did. This fire was located one quarter of a mile west of the intersection of NS122 and EW10. This fire burned 331 acres.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Side Road Fire ignited on the afternoon of February 17, 2026, in Texas County, Oklahoma as a result of dry fuels, low humidity and wind gusts exceeding 60mph. The fire started near U.S. Highway 54, approximately 5 miles west of Tyrone and north of Guymon. This fire started as the result of a seven car accident that occurred on as a result of poor visibility from smoke from the nearby Stevens Fire. The Side Road fire burned 3680 acres. Mandatory evacuations were issued for the community of Tyrone and surrounding areas on February 17th and were lifted on February 21st, and US Highway 54 was closed between Hooker and Tyrone during the height of the fire due to smoke and emergency equipment.  At least six homes were destroyed off Highway 56 and Road D.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Eastern Oklahoma experienced only one widespread rain event in January, as well as a winter storm that affected the area. As a result, total precipitation across the region ranged from half an inch across much of northeastern and east central Oklahoma to four inches in far southeastern Oklahoma. The entire region experienced below average precipitation during the month, with the exception of small portions of Osage County. A lot of the area only received between 25 and 50 percent of normal precipitation for the month. These dry conditions followed a dry November and a very dry December, and resulted in drought conditions developing during January across portions of eastern Oklahoma. Severe (D2) drought conditions developed across much of Choctaw, Mayes, Cherokee, Adair, and Delaware Counties, as well as portions of Pushmataha, Pittsburg, Muskogee, Wagoner, Craig, and Ottawa Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed across portions of Ottawa, Delaware, and Choctaw Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

A low pressure system moving east from off the Mexican Baja coast phased with a strong northern stream low pressure system over the Southern Plains. Precipitation began across eastern Oklahoma during the evening of the 23rd, as these systems approached the area. A couple rounds of heavy wintry precipitation fell across the region through the morning of the 25th. During the first round of precipitation, widespread snow, some heavy, fell north of I-40, with a mixture of sleet and freezing rain south of I-40. The second round began during the evening of the 24th and continued through the morning of the 25th. Heavy snow fell generally north of I-44, with a mixture of heavy sleet and snow south of I-40. Storm totals of up to 12 inches of snow and up to 6 inches of sleet fell across the area. Far southeastern Oklahoma also received up to one quarter of an inch of glaze from freezing rain, before the precipitation changed to sleet and snow.

Eastern Oklahoma experienced only one widespread rain event in January, as well as a winter storm that affected the area. As a result, total precipitation across the region ranged from half an inch across much of northeastern and east central Oklahoma to four inches in far southeastern Oklahoma. The entire region experienced below average precipitation during the month, with the exception of small portions of Osage County. A lot of the area only received between 25 and 50 percent of normal precipitation for the month. An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from September through December 2025 led to the development of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of McCurtain County Oklahoma from the second week of January through the end of the month. During this time, rainfall amounts ranged from 5-8 inches, which was only 25-30% of normal, resulting in considerable hardships from area agricultural producers. Pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires was also noted especially as lower humidities to end the year accelerated the drying of fuels. These conditions only accelerated during December as only a tenth up to a half inch of rain fell during the month throughout the county. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well.

A strong surge of Arctic air invaded Southeast Oklahoma during late January with bitterly cold temperatures and light northerly winds. In wake of the this Arctic air arriving on the evening of January 24th, overnight low temperatures plummeted into the teens by the morning on January 26th and again on the 27th. Although northerly winds were relatively light throughout much of the event, they only further contributed to the dangerously cold temperatures across McCurtain County Oklahoma from late evening on January 25th through late morning on January 27th.

A strong arctic cold front moved south into the Four State Region during the afternoon through the overnight hours on January 23rd-24th, with temperatures quickly falling from the upper 40s to mid 50s on the 23rd into the 20s and lower 30s by the early morning hours on the 24th. Meanwhile, a southwest flow aloft developed over much of the Central and Southern Plains into the Eastern United States, ahead of a large upper level trough that developed along the West Coast and Desert Southwest, and drifted slowly east through the Rockies, Plains, and Mississippi Valley before weakening. This trough tapped ample moisture from the Southern Pacific, with strong overrunning that developed atop the shallow arctic air mass which contributed to widespread periods of freezing rain and sleet across the Four State Region through the morning of the 25th. A strong upper level disturbance and associated cold front translated into the Southern Plains on the 8th. An unseasonably warm and moist air mass had spread into eastern Oklahoma ahead of this system, which resulted in weak instability across the area. A line of thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma from the west during the morning hours of the 8th. Strong wind fields and wind shear associated with the approaching upper level system, combined with the weak instability, supported an environment in which the stronger thunderstorms within the squall line were able to develop low level circulations. One such circulation resulted in a brief, weak tornado and wind gusts to 88 mph in Osage County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado damaged the roofs of several homes, destroyed a large outbuilding, snapped power poles, and blew down trees. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 90 to 100 mph.

Severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 6th, ahead of a surface dry line, and moved across the area through the evening hours. The atmosphere had become strongly unstable across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon east of the dry line. This instability, combined with very strong low-level and deep-layer wind shear across the region, resulted in the evolution of several long-lived supercell thunderstorms. These supercells produced eleven tornadoes, a couple of which were strong and damaging, large hail up to quarter size, damaging wind gusts, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This is the first segment of a two-segment tornado. This tornado developed near N Gilcrease Museum Road, north of W Newton Street. It moved northeast damaging a number of homes, damaging the roof of an apartment complex, uprooting trees, and snapping numerous large tree limbs in neighborhoods west of N Tisdale Parkway. It then crossed into Tulsa County near W Apache Street. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 90 to 100 mph. This tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KINX WSR-88D.

Severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 6th, ahead of a surface dry line, and moved across the area through the evening hours. The atmosphere had become strongly unstable across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon east of the dry line. This instability, combined with very strong low-level and deep-layer wind shear across the region, resulted in the evolution of several long-lived supercell thunderstorms. These supercells produced eleven tornadoes, a couple of which were strong and damaging, large hail up to quarter size, damaging wind gusts, and localized flash flooding.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado developed over heavily wooded, inaccessible (by road) terrain, east of N 161st East Avenue, where the KINX WSR-88D detected a tornadic debris signature. The tornado moved east-northeast across the Caney River, and then destroyed a home and damaged several others south of the river. A large recreational vehicle was rolled and severely damaged. EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began on the west side of Beggs, directly impacting the Beggs Public Schools campus. The High School and Middle School roof sustained significant damage, and the bus barn also suffered heavy damage to the roof and overhead doors. As it moved northeast, it crossed 15th Street, uprooting and snapping trees. After crossing Happy Camp Road, it destroyed outbuildings and began a brief jog northward, paralleling North 180 Road. This strongest and widest phase of the tornado occurred as it moved east along Grimes Road. One single-wide manufactured home was completely destroyed and several other single-family residences were heavily damaged with the loss of roofs and windows. Two fatalities and two injuries occurred at one homestead, where a double-wide manufactured home was completely destroyed and several automobiles were moved and tossed 20 to 30 yards. A nearby barn was destroyed and heavy limb loss occurred on large trees. The tornado then continued northeast, crossing Highway 75, where it threw a metal shipping container across the lanes and uprooted trees. The tornado dissipated after crossing North 205 Road, about three miles south of the Tulsa County line. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 135 to 145 mph. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KINX WSR-88D.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures, very low humidity, gusty southwesterly winds and dry fuels combined to create conditions favorable for fire starts and spread across Oklahoma on the 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Powerline Fire burned 477 acres across far northeastern Hughes County, just west of Dustin. The fire continued to burn into April 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Elevated to near critical fire weather conditions were present on March 5th as southwest winds sustained around 15 to 25 mph and relative humidity values around 15 percent occurred. These conditions, along with continued dry fuels, allowed for a wildfire to occur in Texas County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This fire, named the Unity Corner fire, started from human-related activities during the afternoon hours of March 5th at Mile 20 & Road Q, northwest of Guymon.  It burned 312 acres and was contained within about eight hours with minimal impact to communities and homes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough, centered across the Four Corners, fostered multiple waves of strong-to-severe convection across the WFO Norman Forecast Area during the morning and early evening of the 6th, and again in the early morning of the 7th. Strong mid-tropospheric flow/wind shear and instability yielded a mix of semi-organized convection, including several supercells, during each storm period. Large hail, damaging wind gusts and a tornado (which occurred during the early evening) were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An OKC television storm chaser observed a brief tornado estimated to be approximately 5 miles east-northeast of Little. No damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms extended from Southeast Oklahoma down across Central Texas late in the evening on March 10th, with the most organized threat area over Northeast Texas into Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. Effective storm-relative helicity ahead of the prominent line of thunderstorms was quite favorable for low-level rotation, and instability was rather strong as well. The VAD wind profile from the Shreveport Doppler Radar indicated a very favorable hodograph for rotating storms with 0-1 km storm-relative helicity over 250 m2/s2. As a result, severe thunderstorms produced an isolated tornado and some damaging wind gusts in parts of McCurtain County just prior to midnight on March 10th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The roof was partially peeled back on a home near Garvin.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved into McCurtain County, Oklahoma, late in the evening on March 10th. Circulations were embedded within this line of thunderstorms,  with one of which producing an EF2 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 118 mph that began on Old Golden Highway, resulting in snapped trees and the loss of shingles to a local residence. The tornado then continued east, reaching Thomas Road near the intersection of Old Golden Highway where more trees were snapped and uprooted and a barn/shed experienced damage to the roof. The tornado then began to pick up in intensity as it moved across Oak Hill Road where numerous trees were snapped and uprooted. As the tornado then continued northeast towards Rhoden Road, it caused significant damage to a family residence, resulting in the collapse of most exterior walls and an injury to the occupant who had to be airlifted to the hospital. Trees were then uprooted and fell onto this residence, causing additional damage. Next door to this home, significant damage was found to other structures as well as additional tree damage. Just before reaching Rhoden Road, another residence was damaged, where areas of the roof were uplifted, multiple trees were snapped and uprooted, and the neighboring barn experienced significant roof damage. The tornado then moved north/northeast of the road, pushing a small outbuilding off of its foundation and snapping and uprooting more trees before lifting as it crossed Highway 3.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and northern Oklahoma from the late evening of the 5th into early morning hours of the 6th. This activity developed in the vicinity of a dryline as a deep upper trough began to establish across the Four Coners. As a nocturnal low-level jet strengthened after sunset, a pair of cyclic tornadic thunderstorms emerged from the eastern Texas Panhandle into northern Oklahoma. In addition to several tornadoes, including a deadly tornado west of Fairview in Major County, large hail and eventually damaging wind gusts were observed with severe convection across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations. The report was relayed by emergency management.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, a 63 mph wind gust was recorded at the Idabel Mesonet site.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 63 mph wind gust was measured at the Idabel Mesonet site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of intense damaging winds, associated with a quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) mesovortex, impacted areas from southwest to just north of Marietta. Numerous power poles and trees were damaged along Shady Dale and McGehee Roads southwest of town. Several tractor-trailers were blown over along Interstate 35. The most significant damage occurred near the corner of West Creek Street and South 7th Avenue, where a home lost a significant portion of its roof, causing two exterior walls to collapse. Several businesses near Oklahoma Highway 32 and U.S. Highway 77 had varying degrees of roof damage. Intermittent damage to trees and power poles was also noted in Marietta. The wind path and event time are estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very isolated rain events brought some moisture to the eastern Panhandles during the month. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions worsened across the Oklahoma Panhandle during the month. The month began with the region mostly in Moderate Drought (D1), except for a small area of Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions in northern Cimarron County. Within the first ten days, Severe Drought (D2) expanded to cover the majority of Beaver County. By day 17, two-thirds of Cimarron County, particularly the southwest portion, had also reached D2. Precipitation deficits over the past 120 days, which were already 1 to 2 inches below normal, increased by an additional 1 to 2 inches.

This instability, combined with very strong low-level and deep-layer wind shear across the region, resulted in the evolution of several long-lived supercell thunderstorms. These supercells produced eleven tornadoes, a couple of which were strong and damaging, large hail up to quarter size, damaging wind gusts, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several storm chasers reported thunderstorm wind gusts of 80 to 90 mph on the south side of Pryor.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of McCurtain County Oklahoma through the month of March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged around 2 inches across much of the county, which was only half or less the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Slightly higher amounts closer to 4-5 inches were observed in the far northern portions of the county. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought remained across the southern half of McCurtain County during the entire month.

An upper level system brought showers and thunderstorms during the late afternoon and evening of the 10th across the combined Panhandles. The thunderstorms impacted the northeast but the state of the atmosphere was conducive for strong winds aloft to come down to the surface with even some of the lighter showers and storms. This created a few wind gusts exceeding 58 mph. The next morning on the 11 the upper level system brought high winds to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles creating wind gusts upwards of 71 mph early in the AM hours.

Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed ahead of cold front extending from North Texas into Southeast Oklahoma during the evening of March 4th. Storm organization and mid-level rotation was noted with individual cells in the vicinity of the cold front as it shifted east along the Red River. Effective shear of 30-40 knots and MLCAPE of 1500-2000 J/kg was sufficient to support occasional supercells across the region, with an increasing coverage of storms in response to an associated mid-level shortwave trough ejecting eastward and coupled with a modest strengthening of the low-level jet. One supercell thunderstorm in particular resulted in localized damaging wind gusts in the Sherwood community east of U.S. Highway 259 in McCurtain County Oklahoma, snapping a few pine trees in this area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few snapped softwood trees were reported in the Sherwood community east of Highway 259.

Strong mid-tropospheric flow/wind shear and instability yielded a mix of semi-organized convection, including several supercells, during each storm period. Large hail, damaging wind gusts and a tornado (which occurred during the early evening) were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very dry month of March, with monthly rainfall deficits on the order of one to two inches, led to a continuation of expanding/worsening drought across Oklahoma and western-north Texas.

As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING. The event time was adjusted based on radar observations.

Eastern Oklahoma experienced only one rainfall event during the month of February. During this mid-month event, rainfall across the region ranged from one hundredth to one tenth of an inch across portions of northeastern Oklahoma to as much as three to four inches across portions of east central and southeastern Oklahoma. The rainfall that fell across eastern Oklahoma in February was below the monthly average amounts for much of the region, with a large portion of northeastern Oklahoma only receiving from one to five percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. These very dry conditions, compounding on several months of dry weather, allowed the drought that developed across portions of the region in January to expand in February. Severe (D2) drought conditions developed across all of Washington, Nowata, Craig, Ottawa, Rogers, Mayes, Delaware, Wagoner, and Cherokee Counties, and developed across portions of Tulsa, Muskogee, Adair, McIntosh, Pittsburg, Pushmataha, and Choctaw Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed into portions of Choctaw, Ottawa, Delaware, Mayes, Wagoner, Cherokee, Muskogee and Adair Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of McCurtain County Oklahoma through the month of February. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 1.50-2.50 inches,  which was only half or less the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought had expanded across the southern half of McCurtain County during the final few weeks of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impactful and long-duration winter storm impacted Oklahoma and western-north Texas beginning on the evening of the 23rd and lasting into the morning of the 25th. A strong surface high, with origins across far northern latitudes, ushered in a very cold/sub-freezing airmass across the region by the morning of the 23rd. Over the coming 36 hours, increasingly strong west-southwesterly flow (and associated lift) fostered multiple waves of frozen precipitation across the forecast area. Initially, a mix of snow and sleet occurred, owing to a notable warm layer (i.e., warm nose) located between 700 and 800 mb. Eventually, by Saturday evening, continued mid-level cooling allowed for a transition to mostly snow with continued precipitation into Sunday morning. ||While individual event narratives are not included for Cotton, Harmon, Harper, Jefferson, Love and Tillman Counties, with no direct surface observations reported during the event, at least 2 inches of snow/sleet accumulations and slick roadways likely occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The county received a combination of snow and sleet during this event, producing 4 to 10 inches of accumulation. The highest observed total (9.5 inches) was reported near Prague. Listed amounts reflect a synthesis of both remote sensing and direct observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. This winter storm brought mostly snow to the region, but also there was some sleet mixed in across the southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle during the onset of precipitation across the region. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Frigid temperatures were also associated with this system and wind chill values dropped to as low as -20 to -25��F in the early morning hours during this time period. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. The combination of the dangerously cold temperatures and impactful snowfall led to the closure of multiple school districts across the region as well as businesses and local government buildings. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One to two inches of snow fell across the county. Boise City measured around 1.5 inches of snow. An additional few tenths fell the morning of January 25th.
